content: Yoga, derived from the Sanskrit term yuj, meaning to control, to yoke, or to unite, refers to a collection of ancient spiritual practices originating in India. These practices are designed to achieve spiritual insight, self-discipline, and a profound understanding of existence. Gavin Flood, an academic authority on Hindu studies, describes yoga as a set of techniques or disciplines involving asceticism and meditation, which aim to lead practitioners to spiritual experiences and deep existential insights. Yoga is deeply intertwined with the religious beliefs and practices of Indian religions, including Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism. Outside India, yoga is often associated with physical postures (asanas) from Hatha Yoga or as a form of exercise. However, its influence extends far beyond physical practice, shaping spiritual traditions globally. Hindu texts such as the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, and the Shiva Samhita discuss various aspects of yoga. Major branches of yoga include Hatha Yoga, Karma Yoga (yoga of action), Jnana Yoga (yoga of knowledge), Bhakti Yoga (yoga of devotion), and Raja Yoga (yoga of meditation and mental control). Raja Yoga, as outlined in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, is one of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy and focuses on controlling the mind to achieve liberation. The history of yoga can be traced back to the Indus Valley Civilization (circa 3300–1700 BCE), where seals depicting figures in meditative postures have been discovered. Archaeologist Gregory Possehl suggests these images represent early forms of ritual discipline, possibly precursors to yoga. The Pashupati seal, discovered by John Marshall, has been interpreted by some as depicting a proto-Shiva figure in a yoga posture, though this interpretation remains speculative. In the Upanishads, early references to meditation and ascetic practices (tapas) appear, with the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (circa 900 BCE) being one of the earliest texts to mention meditation. The Bhagavad Gita (circa 200 BCE), a key text within the Mahabharata, extensively discusses yoga in various forms, emphasizing Karma Yoga, Bhakti Yoga, and Jnana Yoga. Commentators like Madhusudana Sarasvati have divided the Gita into sections corresponding to these three paths. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (circa 200 BCE–300 CE) form the foundational text of classical yoga philosophy. Patanjali defines yoga as the cessation of mental fluctuations, emphasizing mental discipline and meditation. His system, known as Raja Yoga, outlines an eight-limbed path (Ashtanga Yoga) that includes ethical principles (yamas and niyamas), physical postures (asanas), breath control (pranayama), sensory withdrawal (pratyahara), concentration (dharana), meditation (dhyana), and ultimate absorption (samadhi). This framework provides a comprehensive guide to achieving liberation (kaivalya). Hatha Yoga, as described in the 15th-century text Hatha Yoga Pradipika by Yogi Swatmarama, focuses on physical purification (shatkarmas) and the regulation of vital energy (prana) as a means to mental and spiritual purification. Unlike Raja Yoga, which begins with mental discipline, Hatha Yoga emphasizes the body through asanas and pranayama. It also incorporates tantric elements, introducing concepts like chakras and kundalini energy. Modern Hatha Yoga, with its emphasis on physical postures, is the form most commonly associated with yoga in the West. Yoga has also influenced other traditions, such as Buddhism. In Yogacara Buddhism (4th–5th centuries CE), yoga serves as a framework for practices leading to enlightenment. Zen Buddhism, derived from the Sanskrit term dhyana (meditation), shares similarities with yoga, particularly in its meditative practices. Tibetan Buddhism incorporates yoga into its spiritual practices, progressing through stages like Mahayoga, Anuyoga, and Atiyoga, with advanced techniques involving breath, movement, and visualization. Tantric traditions also integrate yoga, emphasizing practices that transcend ordinary social and religious norms. Tantra views reality as an illusion (maya) and seeks liberation through techniques like chakra meditation and kundalini yoga, aiming to awaken and channel spiritual energy. The ultimate goal of yoga varies across traditions. In Advaita Vedanta and Shaivism, the goal is moksha, or liberation from worldly suffering and the cycle of birth and death (samsara), culminating in unity with the Supreme Brahman. In Bhakti traditions, the goal is eternal devotion and a personal relationship with a deity, such as Vishnu, Krishna, or Rama. For many modern practitioners, yoga serves as a means to improve physical health, mental well-being, and spiritual growth.
